The twenty second check, before every send

  1. Open the profile. Confirm the title and company still match the row.
  2. Read Experience. If a past employer is a current Hustad client and their time there overlaps our work, switch to Shared history, put that company where [CLIENT] sits, type it in the past employer box, and send it yourself.
  3. If their current company is a Hustad account, skip and note it. That is warm outreach and it runs elsewhere.
  4. If they replied on an earlier touch, tick Replied. Their later touches stop automatically.
  5. Paste, send, tick Sent. The log writes itself.

Order is deliberate: follow ups first, then first touches. If the hour runs short, defer first touches rather than rush a live conversation.

Cold new business only. Hustad does not do ground up construction and nothing here pitches it. Past employment at a Hustad client is your own opener, never a handoff. Every message is sent by hand. Decision styles: match the reply to the reader

Analytical verifier

Tells: Asks for definitions, backup, sample reports, what is included and excluded, how the grade is calculated, comparability across vendors. Longer messages with specific questions.

AdjustName the evidence basis and offer the backup: summary first, detail available. Answer the exact question asked before anything else. Never round or generalize.

In practice

Good question. The grade is set per roof section from documented condition and remaining useful life, not age alone, and every finding carries a photo and a price. I can send the two page summary plus the full appendix behind it so you can see how the numbers roll up. Which would you rather see first?

Decisive controller

Tells: Short replies, fast, wants the point, asks what the next step is, uses imperatives (send it, set it up, who do I talk to).

AdjustBottom line in sentence one. CTA carries an owner and a date. No preamble.

In practice

Next step: a 15 minute call with {hustad_owner} on Thursday at 10 or 2 Central. I will send the sample report before the call so it is a decision, not a demo. Which time?

Risk shield

Tells: Asks about warranties, insurance, documentation, what could go wrong, liability, who is responsible, what happens if.

AdjustName what is preserved: small reversible first step, options kept open, documentation as protection. No promises on outcomes.

In practice

The first step is reversible: one inspection with photos and a graded report. Nothing gets repaired without your approval, the cap is a ceiling not a bill, and the report is yours to keep whichever way you go. Would one property be a reasonable place to start?

Consensus builder

Tells: Mentions ownership, a committee, regionals, the VP, needs to run it by someone, asks for something to share.

AdjustSwap the call for a forwardable one pager they can send up without translating. Offer to write the internal summary.

In practice

Makes sense. I will send a one page summary written for the people you need to bring along: what the program is, what it costs to start, and what changes for the site teams. If it helps, I can draft the two lines you would use to introduce it internally. Who else needs to feel comfortable before this moves?

Operational protector

Tells: Talks about site teams, residents, disruption, access, noise, leasing season, turn, staff burden.

AdjustName quiet execution and sequencing before anything else. Show the site team gains time, not work.

In practice

The sequencing comes first: inspections are scheduled with the site, crews check in with the office, work zones are set so residents keep their access, and small repairs happen while the crew is already there so the site is not chasing a second visit. The report goes to you, not to the site team to interpret. Would that fit how your properties run?

Price led comparator

Tells: Mentions bids, numbers, help me compare, what your rates are, we bid everything.

AdjustName scope clarity and what a low number usually excludes. Never lead with price. Offer the leveling example.

In practice

Comparing is the right move, and the useful comparison is scope, not the bottom line. Two roof proposals at the same price can describe different work, and the low one usually wins on what it left out. I can send a one page example of three bids leveled to one scope so you can see how that plays out. Useful?

Skeptical scar tissue

Tells: References a prior vendor failure, we have heard this before, every roofer says that, burned before.

AdjustOpen with what we know and what we do not know. Make the smallest claim in the library. Offer one property as the test.

In practice

Understood, and you should be skeptical. What we know is how we document and price; what we do not know is whether your roofs need any of it. One property, one inspection, one report. If it tells you nothing new, that is the answer and I will not push. Worth one?

Buyer states, and the one question per message rule

Calm evaluator

Cues: Full sentences, good questions, no time panic, replies within a day or two.

AdjustStructured reply, tradeoffs allowed, can carry a slightly larger ask (a 15 minute call).

Compressed and overloaded

Cues: Short replies, long silence then a burst, asks for the bottom line, replies at odd hours.

AdjustCut to 40 words. Bottom line first. One binary question. Separate now from later.

Guarded and skeptical

Cues: Asks what is excluded, references a prior vendor, wants proof before talk.

AdjustLead with what we know and what we do not know yet. Offer proof, never push it. Smallest possible claim.

Anxious and loss focused

Cues: Mentions active damage, residents, premiums, a deadline.

AdjustContainment first, options second, one small reversible step. Route to a call fast. Zero selling.

Consensus builder

Cues: Mentions a regional, ownership, a committee, or needs to run it by someone.

AdjustOffer a forwardable one pager instead of a meeting. Make their internal job easy.

Ready to move

Cues: Asks for schedule, scope, or who shows up.

AdjustDrop the sequence. Be decisive: owner, date, next step. Confirm timing and remove friction.

Qualification, one per message

  1. Scope: How many properties or units does your team cover, and in which markets? Sizes the program and picks the regional team.
  2. Ownership of the decision: Who owns roof and exterior decisions at {company_short}: regional ops, facilities, asset management, or ownership? Multi-threading map. Names the second contact.
  3. Current state: How are roof inspections handled today: a vendor program, in house walks, or mostly when something leaks? Reveals reactive versus proactive and the incumbent.
  4. Pain: What did the last 12 months of roof spend look like: mostly leak calls and emergency dispatches, or planned work? Loss aversion framed factually; sets the value story.
  5. Timing: When do next year's capital numbers lock, and is there a turn or leasing window we should plan around? Sets the calendar and the why now.
  6. Format preference: Would one recommendation help more, or two options with tradeoffs? Playbook question; reveals decision style.
  7. Committee: Who else needs to feel comfortable before a program like this moves? Playbook question; reveals consensus needs.

Content engagement: replies in public

The categories above answer outreach. These cover people who engage with a post before any DM goes out, which are the warmest contacts the program produces and the only ones whose replies their whole network can see. No templates on purpose: a comment reply that reads like it came from a library is worse than staying quiet.

Substantive comment on our post

Do thisAnswer inside 90 minutes while the post is live. Agree with the specific thing they said, then add the one thing they did not have. Their comment is the setup; the value is what you know that they do not, from the exterior side.

Discipline: Never list obvious tactical items. Match their altitude: someone writing about systems gets an answer about systems. No pitch, no link, no company name unless it carries the point. Then DM the same day referencing the exchange.

They post something in our lane and we are the guest

Do thisComment on their post, not just their comment on ours. Their audience is our audience, and contributing on their turf is worth more reach than posting our own.

Discipline: Contribute one idea, take responsibility where the vendor side owns the problem, and sell nothing. Do not mirror their sentence rhythm, especially if they write in the constructions our own standards ban.

DM after they engaged with content

Do thisOpen by naming the exchange so they can place you, agree with their point, then describe how we actually run it (docs/SERVICE_DELIVERY.md), then one give. Client names carry real weight here: the cleared list is Asset Living, Cardinal Group, Campus Life and Style, Dial Retirement Communities and Burlington Capital, plus regional relationships Eric names himself.

Discipline: Longer than a cold first touch is fine when they wrote at length; matching their depth reads as respect. Still one ask, still the give first, still no pricing.

They reshare or quote our content

Do thisThank them in the thread in one line, and look at who engaged with their reshare. A reshare puts our material in front of a network we did not have.

Discipline: No ask attached to a thank you. If someone in their network engaged too, that is a separate first touch, run through the normal gates.

What to give someone who engaged

  1. The sample property record, redacted: what one building's documentation actually looks like.
  2. The post storm documentation sequence, one page, baseline through closeout.
  3. The Exterior Risk File newsletter, if the topic they engaged on is the month's theme.

Objections, answered short

Why inspect now instead of waiting?

Answer

Because the small items are cheap now and expensive after the first freeze or the first storm. The inspection also puts a documented baseline in the file before budgets lock, which is when the roof line gets argued about.

Why fix something that is not leaking yet?

Answer

Non leaking items like lifted seams, loose flashing and failed sealant are exactly what manufacturers classify as owner maintenance. Leave them and the warranty conversation gets harder; fix them in the inspection visit and it costs a fraction of the leak call.

How is this different from normal wear?

Answer

Normal wear is expected and graded. What we flag is the wear that has reached the point where water follows it inside, and we show the photo so you can judge it yourself.

What is the downside of deferring to budget season?

Answer

Deferred items get repriced, usually higher, and some of them become interior events in the meantime. The proposal expires; the problem does not.

What is included and excluded in your inspection?

Answer

Included: every roof section photographed, graded A to F, deficiencies priced, drains and penetrations checked, warranty checkpoints logged. Excluded: destructive testing and engineering opinions, which we will tell you when a roof needs them.

What makes your bid different from the low number?

Answer

Scope. Our proposals separate base scope, unit price items, change order triggers, warranty path and owner responsibilities so you can see what the low number left out. We are glad to be leveled against anyone on the same scope.

How do warranties work after installation?

Answer

A system warranty covers membrane and approved workmanship; a membrane only warranty covers the material. Both require documented inspections and completed owner maintenance items to stay in force. We build that record annually. Specific coverage is always per the manufacturer's document.

What happens when reality changes in the field?

Answer

Concealed conditions are documented with photos before anything is done, priced against the unit rates in the proposal, and approved before work continues. No surprises on the invoice.

Do you do new construction?

Answer

No. We work on buildings that are already standing: inspections, service and maintenance, storm response, and capital roof and exterior work on occupied properties. If you are building something new, we are not your contractor, and I will say so rather than waste your time.

We already have a roofer.

Answer

Most portfolios do, and plenty of them are fine. The question is usually whether you have a current condition read per building, or whether you have a phone number you call when something leaks. If it is the first one, you do not need us. If it is the second, that is the gap we fill.

Are you licensed where our properties are?

Answer

Tell me the states and I will confirm before we go any further. We are not going to pretend to cover a market we cannot service properly.

The posting week

Four slots: Tuesday a personal point of view, Wednesday the designed asset, Thursday the long companion tied to the month’s newsletter or article, Saturday the human one. Carousels go out on the personal profile and the company page reshares them; the stat and checklist cards run on the company page and Eric reshares those. Copy the text, download or print the asset, post at the time on the chip, tick Posted, paste the live URL. Links go in the first comment, never the body.

The fifteen minutes around a postTen minutes before: comment on three to five posts from operators and facilities people, so the algorithm sees a participant, not a broadcaster. The first ninety minutes after: answer every comment; early replies are what carry a post to second degree feeds. The DM desk and this calendar are one system: forty people a day open Eric’s profile after a DM, and these posts are what they find there.

Week of Aug 31

The exterior line in most 2027 budgets is last year's number plus a percentage. The roof does not know that.

Tue 2026-09-01PersonalText8:15 AM CTBudget season opens
Post text

Budget season opened this week. Over the next eight weeks, exterior numbers get set for thousands of buildings, and most of them will be built the same way: take last year, add escalation, move on.

The alternative is a condition read. Which roofs are holding, which are aging, which small items become interior events by spring. It changes the argument from a percentage to a photograph.

When the committee pushes back on a number built from age and invoices, there is nothing to point at. When it pushes back on a documented condition, the documents answer.

How does your team build the exterior number: a current condition read, or age and invoices?

Assumed life is not a plan. Two roofs installed the same year diverge fast on drainage, traffic and maintenance. One goes 25 years, its twin goes 14, and the spreadsheet said 20 for both.

The Exterior Risk File

How exterior condition, documentation and capital planning connect on occupied properties. Written for portfolio executives, asset managers and facilities leaders.

Monthly, first Thursday, published 8:00 AM CT. LinkedIn newsletters cannot be published by API; issue day is a ten minute manual publish from this draft.

Issue 1: The Exterior Risk File

Subject: The eight records that end roof arguments

2026-09-03Full draft
Draft

Every portfolio has a story about the roof that surprised them. The leak that turned out to be three years of deferred flashing. The warranty that lapsed on paperwork. The capital plan that budgeted a replacement for the wrong building. Different stories, same root: the information existed once, and nobody could put a hand on it when it mattered.

This newsletter is about the file that catches those stories before they happen. Not software, not a program you buy. A folder, kept current, per building. Eight records.

One. A condition grade per building, A to F, set from documented condition and remaining useful life rather than age. A roof's age says when it went on. What it has been through since is the part the plan actually needs.

Two. The repair versus capital split. Every open finding classified: maintenance dollars this year, or capital plan. The split is a decision, and making it in the file beats making it in a hallway during budget week.

Three. A photo record tied to dates. Roof by roof, visit by visit. Most exterior disputes are chronology disputes, and dated photographs end chronology disputes.

Four. Warranty terms next to the maintenance they require. Coverage stays alive through documented owner maintenance. Keep the obligations where the maintenance schedule can see them, not in a drawer with the closing documents.

Five. A storm log with sources. When a verified event touches a market, the file gets the weather record and the post event walk, even when the note is clean. Building that record the week of the event costs a morning. Rebuilding it in February costs weeks and comes back incomplete.

Six. Open items, priced. An unpriced deficiency is invisible to a budget. Priced, it becomes a decision someone owns: fix, defer knowingly, or capital.

Seven. Closeout records. Every completed project ends with as built scope, final photos, warranty registration and punch closure. The closeout is the first record in the next capital plan.

Eight. The one page summary. Everything above, per building, on a page a committee can read. The appendix holds the detail; the page holds the decision.

None of this requires a particular vendor, including us. It requires an honest afternoon to find out what you hold, and a cadence to keep it current. Next month: why most inspection reports fail the file, and the one page format that fixes them.

Issue 2: Why Inspection Reports Need a Decision Section

Subject: The missing page in the forty page roof report

2026-10-01Full draft
Draft

The forty page roof report is a familiar object: photos, thermal images, a condition narrative, sometimes a core cut. Then it ends. The reader is left holding descriptions, and the decision the report was commissioned to inform has not moved an inch.

A report is finished when a person who was not on the roof can make a decision from it. That standard produces a structural fix: every finding carries four lines.

Condition. What was found, graded, photographed, dated. The grade does the comparative work a narrative cannot: a D next to a B is an argument settled before it starts.

Consequence. What happens if nothing is done, stated plainly. Water tracks behind the membrane and reaches the ceiling cavity with the first hard freeze. No adjectives. The reader can weigh a consequence; they cannot weigh 'concerning'.

Cost. The number for fixing it now, and the class of number it becomes later. Not a scare figure: a classification. Maintenance line now, remediation plus repair after the freeze.

Recommendation. One sentence, committed to in writing. Repair within 30 days under the standing cap. This is the line most reports omit, because committing is a risk. It is also the entire value of having an expert on the roof.

Multiply the four lines by every open item and the report becomes an instrument: the repair versus capital split falls out of it, the priced open items list falls out of it, and the one page summary writes itself.

Five questions tell you whether a report you are holding meets the standard. Is every finding graded, photographed and dated. Is each item split repair versus capital. Is there a price next to every open item. Is there a written recommendation. Could someone who never saw the roof make the call from this.

If the answer to the last one is no, the gap belongs to the report, not to you. Next month: warranty as a workflow, and the five documents that keep coverage alive.

Issue 3: Warranty Is a Workflow

Subject: The coverage you keep by doing the boring things

2026-11-05Outline, write from thesis
Committed outline

Thesis: a roof warranty is a workflow with owner obligations, and coverage erodes quietly when the workflow stops. Sections: what manufacturer warranties actually require of owners; the five document warranty file (warranty registered, obligations as a checklist, annual inspection reports, small item repair records, correspondence log); how the annual documented inspection doubles as the file's heartbeat; what erosion looks like in practice, told as patterns not cases; the workflow calendar. Caveat everywhere: specific coverage is always per the manufacturer's document. No coverage promises.

Issue 4: The Difference Between a Repair Budget and a Capital Plan

Subject: One answers this year. The other answers the next ten.

2026-12-03Outline, write from thesis
Committed outline

Thesis: repair budgets are real and owned; capital plans are often installation date spreadsheets, and condition graded plans reallocate the same total to better outcomes. Sections: how age based plans miss diverging twins; what a condition based plan looks like per line; the recurring repair signal that flags hidden capital items; how closeouts keep the plan current; the December conversation with ownership, and what to bring to it. Draws on the NRCA 25 year case study with the source attached.

Issue 5: The Cost of a Missing Closeout

Subject: Projects that never ended, and what they cost later

2027-01-07Outline, write from thesis
Committed outline

Thesis: the closeout package is an afternoon at project end and weeks of reconstruction years later; its absence surfaces at sales, warranty tests and rebids. Sections: the five part closeout package; the sale scenario, the warranty scenario, the rebid scenario as patterns; closeout as the first record of the next capital plan; a January exercise, closing out last year's projects while memories are fresh.

Issue 6: The Next Standard for Exterior Asset Management

Subject: The system, assembled

2027-02-04Outline, write from thesis
Committed outline

Thesis: the five prior issues assemble into one standard: graded condition, decision ready reporting, live warranty files, storm discipline, closed loops. Synthesis issue, no new claims. Sections: the standard on one page; what adopting it costs, honestly, in hours and cadence; what it changes for each seat, asset manager, facilities lead, site team; where the industry is heading and what to watch. Ends the six month arc and asks readers what the next arc should cover.

The pitch week

  1. Monday: pick the week’s one objective, an article, a pitch, or an interview.
  2. Tuesday: draft or edit the asset. Angle, title, source list, bio, headshot ready.
  3. Wednesday: send up to three personalized pitches. Log each one here.
  4. Thursday: publish or promote the owned companion. Engage on LinkedIn.
  5. Friday: follow up on pitches older than seven business days. Update statuses below.

One outlet at a time per article. Original work only. Statuses here move with you and stay saved.

Repurposing, after each publication

  1. Every published article becomes: two LinkedIn posts, one carousel, one short video, one internal sales talking point.
  2. Never publish the article itself on the Hustad site before the outlet does; write a companion instead.
  3. After publication: add the live link here, to the media sheet, and to the insights hub.
  4. One outlet at a time per article. Original work only.
